AI Product Design · Case Study

Guru AI — helping fundraisers act, not dig.

Atlas is a donor-management app for Catholic church organizations. Staff had thousands of donor records but acted on only a few — the useful signals were buried. I designed Guru AI: ask a question in plain English, get a list of the right donors, and act on it right there — build a report, open a profile, or send an outreach email. Here's the story.

My role
AI Product Design — research & design
Collaborators
PM, Engineering, Design Manager
Timeline

Outcome
From a question to action in one place

Understanding the product

Atlas helps churches track donors and donations. But a single "diocese" is really hundreds of smaller churches and funds, each with its own money and rules — so the data is huge and scattered. Fundraisers spend their day entering gifts, following up with donors, and trying to answer questions like "who should I call today?"

The answers were hidden in the data, and getting them meant building a report or exporting to Excel. Most people didn't have the time — so good donors slipped through the cracks.

Why was this prioritized?

Two things were happening at once. Fundraisers were missing chances — they'd only notice a donor had stopped giving when it was too late. And the team was drowning in manual work: pulling the same reports every week just to find a handful of people to contact.

Keeping donors is where the money is. A few percent more retention on a large base is real, recurring income. An assistant that surfaced the right people — and let staff act in the same place — would pay for itself.

The challenges I had to solve

Guru AI wasn't just "add a chatbot." To actually improve the Atlas experience it had to clear six bars:

01

Find people without a report

Let a non-technical user get the exact right donors by just asking — no filters, no report builder.

02

Earn trust about money

Answers must be grounded in real records and show their reasoning — never invent a donor's giving.

03

Turn an answer into action

A list is only useful if you can act on it: open a profile, build a report, or email the group — in one place.

04

Stay inside permissions

Guru can only use data the user may already see, so it never leaks one parish's donor money to another.

05

Cut the busywork

Remove the Excel export → re-import → mail-merge detour that ate afternoons.

06

Close the loop

Acting on a donor should update their record, so the next answer is fresh and the list keeps itself clean.

I started with one rule

AI points. The human decides.

Guru surfaces patterns, summarizes, drafts, and answers over your own data. It never decides who to ask for money, moves money, or messages a donor on its own. Anything that broke this rule didn't ship.

Idea #1 — just a chat box

The obvious first move was a chat assistant: type a question, get an answer. It worked, but testing showed the same thing users warned about — people opened it, stared at the empty prompt, and closed it.

Why it fell short
  • It put the hard part — knowing what to ask — back on the user.
  • Busy fundraisers won't "explore" an AI; they want it to tell them what matters.
Proof: in task tests, most users couldn't think of a useful first question unprompted — the blank prompt had the lowest task-completion of anything we tried.

Idea #2 — bring the insight to them

So I flipped it. Instead of waiting to be asked, Guru does the noticing and shows the day's few high-value moves right on the dashboard. Each says what it found, why (the evidence), and gives a one-tap action.

Proof: once the insight carried its reason ("gave last April, nothing yet this year"), reviewers stopped asking "is this right?" and started asking "who's on the list?" — the sign trust had landed.

Idea #3 — make the answer a list you can act on

An insight or a question is only half the job. The breakthrough was treating every Guru answer as a working list of donors — not a dead-end chat reply. From that list you can open anyone's profile, turn the whole group into a report, or email them, without leaving the page.

Ask Guru→Donor list→Open profile/Generate report/Send outreach

One query, end to end

Here's a real example a fundraiser runs all the time: "Top donors by parish who haven't been contacted in 90 days." Watch how far one question goes.

Step 1 — Ask, and get the right people

A plain-English question becomes a precise list

Guru reads the question, shows how it understood it, and returns 18 donors — grounded in the real data, sorted by who's been ignored longest. No filters, no report builder.

Step 2 — Open anyone to get the full picture

One click to a donor's profile

Before reaching out, the fundraiser opens a donor. Everything they need to make it personal is there: contact details, household and relationships, and the full giving history.

Step 3 — Turn the list into a report

The same list, now a shareable report

Need to brief a pastor or the board? The list becomes a full report in one click — the same self-serve report page, no analyst required.

Step 4 — Message the whole group

Outreach, with the busywork removed

Or act now: the whole list becomes a personalized email, contact details already attached. Each donor gets their own name and parish merged in — no Excel, no copy-paste.

Why this matters: the afternoon-long "find → export → mail-merge" chore collapses into a few clicks — and because sending updates each donor's "last contact," they drop off the 90-day list automatically. The loop closes itself.

Designing for trust

Across all of it, trust was the material I cared about most. Guru only answers from your own records, shows its reasoning, links to the source, and marks anything consequential as a suggestion a human confirms. When it can't ground an answer, it says so instead of guessing — a graceful "I don't know" beats a confident wrong number, especially about money.

The all-new Guru experience

✓Tells you what needs you today

✓Answers plain-English questions

Impact & how I'd measure it

Because every insight and answer turns into an in-app action, success is measurable. I'd watch whether people act on the lists (not just see them), whether Excel exports drop (the tool is now enough), whether outreach volume and speed go up, and whether lapsed donors come back. Guardrails: the "wrong answer" rate stays low, and Guru never shows donor money across church boundaries it shouldn't.
